papers.title: Simultaneous Two-Photon Calcium Imaging, Electroencephalography, and Electromyography with Intracortical Electrical Stimulation in Freely Moving Mice.
papers.abstract: Simultaneously combining cellular-resolution imaging, electrical neuromodulation, and electrophysiological monitoring in freely moving mice requires a mechanically stable chronic implant and precise synchronization across recording systems. This protocol describes an integrated preparation for cortical two-photon calcium imaging, intracortical electrical stimulation, electroencephalography (EEG), and electromyography (EMG) in freely moving, tethered mice. Using the retrosplenial cortex as an example target, the protocol details fabrication and implantation of the cranial window and electrodes, viral delivery, optical field localization, installation of a detachable imaging interface, behavioral habituation, multimodal data acquisition, and stimulation-aligned calcium-signal analysis. The preparation permits repeated optical access over short- and long-term intervals and generates cellular-resolution calcium signals together with concurrent electrophysiological and motor-state measurements. Representative outputs include continuous multimodal session-level recordings, mouse-level population calcium responses, and paired stimulation-off and stimulation-on response measures. The workflow can be adapted to other experimentally accessible cortical targets by modifying the cranial-window location, viral injection coordinates, electrode trajectory, and implant geometry.

papers.title: Sleep EEG distinguishes learned from novel auditory cues without predicting memory retention in a targeted memory reactivation study
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

papers.title: Experimental Sleep Manipulation and Pain Sensitivity in Healthy Adults: A Focused Review with Emphasis on Sleep Fragmentation.
papers.abstract: Experimental sleep loss can increase pain sensitivity, but sleep duration, continuity, and architecture are often altered simultaneously. This focused review compared pain outcomes across experimental sleep manipulations in healthy adults, with particular attention to sleep fragmentation (SF) and related awakening paradigms. PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection were searched through 16 September 2026; reference and citation checking identified additional reports. Eligible reports were synthesized narratively by sleep manipulation, design, pain modality, and dynamic pain-processing outcome. Designs included randomized or counterbalanced crossover studies, other within-participant or repeated-measures experiments, and parallel-group studies. Fifty-two reports met the eligibility criteria. After overlapping and nested publications were consolidated, they formed 40 publication families comprising 41 provisionally distinct participant samples and approximately 1083 participants with analyzable data. Non-mutually exclusive categories comprised 21 reports of total sleep deprivation (TSD) or prolonged wakefulness, 17 of partial sleep restriction (PSR) or night-shift exposure, two directly evaluating SF, 10 evaluating related planned- or forced-awakening paradigms, six evaluating selective sleep-stage disruption, and two reports from provisionally distinct samples evaluating combined short and disrupted sleep. TSD and PSR showed the broadest evidence of increased pain sensitivity, but effects varied by modality and outcome. Both direct-SF reports identified at least one hyperalgesic outcome; the awakening literature was suggestive but contained multiple reports from shared samples. The combined protocol did not isolate sleep continuity from reduced duration. Disrupted sleep continuity may contribute to hyperalgesia, but an independent effect of SF remains uncertain because direct evidence is limited and awakening protocols often also change sleep duration, architecture, stress, or circadian timing.

papers.title: Revisiting the First Night Effect of Polysomnography Using Wearable EEG Headbands in Older Adults with Sleep Disturbances
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The first night effect (FNE), where sleep is altered during the first night of polysomnography (PSG), may affect the validity of single-night PSG assessments, yet its magnitude relative to habitual sleep is difficult to characterize using repeated PSG alone. We examined FNE during home-based PSG (HPSG) in older adults with sleep disturbances using multi-night wearable EEG headband (HB) recordings. Methods: Fifty-eight community-dwelling adults aged 55-85 years with sleep disturbances completed up to seven nights of HB monitoring, including one night of simultaneous HPSG. Using HB-derived measures, we compared total sleep time (TST), wake after sleep onset (WASO), sleep efficiency (SE), minutes in N3 sleep, and minutes in REM sleep between HPSG and non-HPSG nights via pairwise comparisons and linear mixed-effects models adjusting for age, sex, and race/ethnicity. Results: Sleep differed significantly between HPSG and non-HPSG nights, with roughly 35 minutes longer WASO, 21 minutes less N3 sleep, and 15% lower SE (ps < .001) during HPSG nights. TST and REM sleep did not differ between HPSG and non-HPSG nights. Findings were consistent when separately comparing nights preceding and following HPSG. Conclusions: In older adults with sleep disturbances, a single night of HPSG was associated with greater wake after sleep onset, less N3 sleep, and lower sleep efficiency than other nights measured with wearable EEG, suggesting that one-night PSG may overstate sleep disruption and understate deep sleep. Multi-night wearable EEG monitoring may help assess the representativeness of single-night PSG measurements, thereby improving the accuracy of sleep measurement interpretation.

papers.title: Swimming Toward Recovery: Early Aquatic Therapy as a Bridge to Delayed Environmental Enrichment After Experimental Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) is a well-established preclinical model of neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI). However, most paradigms initiate EE immediately after injury and provide it continuously, unlike clinical rehabilitation, which is typically delayed until medical stabilization and delivered for defined periods. We hypothesized that early aquatic therapy (AQT), an exercise-based intervention, would enhance the benefits of delayed EE, providing a rehabilitative bridge during the early post-injury period. Adult male rats received a cortical impact or sham injury and were housed under standard (STD) conditions. Beginning 1 day after surgery, bridge groups received daily AQT for 7 days, while comparison groups remained in STD housing. On post-injury day 8, EE (6 h/day) was initiated in bridge and EE-only groups. Motor, cognitive, and anxiety-like behaviors were assessed. AQT alone and AQT + EE improved motor performance versus STD (p < 0.05), with AQT + EE producing the fewest foot slips and outperforming EE alone. EE improved spatial learning, while AQT + EE produced the strongest acquisition among TBI groups (p < 0.05); memory retention improved only in EE-treated groups. AQT + EE outperformed STD on the first and third reversal stages of executive function, whereas EE alone outperformed STD on the third reversal. Reduced anxiety-like behavior occurred only in EE-treated groups. Overall, the hypothesis was partially supported as sequential AQT + EE produced greater improvements than EE alone on selected motor, spatial learning, and executive outcomes, but EE alone improved memory retention and anxiety-like behavior. These findings support early AQT as a rehabilitative bridge to delayed EE and warrant further investigation of staged rehabilitation paradigms after TBI.

papers.title: Phosphorylation-dependent ATPase activity regulates subunit shuffling dynamics in cyanobacterial circadian clock proteins.
papers.abstract: Protein complexes are essential for cellular functions, with their dynamics increasingly recognized as key regulatory elements. In the cyanobacterial circadian clock, the KaiC hexamer is highly dynamic, undergoing phosphorylation-dependent monomer shuffling that synchronizes individual oscillators. However, the molecular mechanism of monomer shuffling is not fully understood. Here we combine a chromatography-based method with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to quantify subunit exchange in the hexamerization domain of KaiC (KaiC-CI) and in full-length KaiC. We show that ATPase activity is essential for monomer shuffling. Through quantitative modeling of experimental data, we found that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis at two independent monomer-monomer interfaces disassembles a KaiC-CI hexamer into two oligomers. Two complementary oligomers from two different hexamers can rapidly reform a mixed hexamer. Mechanistically, ATP hydrolysis induces unstable, shuffling-competent states in hexamers, while nucleotide exchange stabilizes them, suppressing shuffling. The balance between these two processes quantitatively explains the relationship between shuffling rate and ATPase activity across KaiC mutants observed in our experiments. Applying this model to full-length KaiC revealed that phosphorylation of the KaiC-CII domain modulates shuffling primarily by affecting the nucleotide exchange rate in the CI domain. This establishes a feedback loop where CII phosphorylation alters CI ATPase activity, which in turn controls subunit exchange to synchronize CII phosphorylation across the KaiC hexamer population. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework linking ATPase-driven subunit exchange to the robustness of circadian clocks, with implications for activation-coupled dynamics in other molecular machines.

papers.title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
papers.abstract: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.

papers.title: Adult EEG Reactivity in Rat Offspring After an Uncomplicated Birth Is Not Significantly Altered by Gestational Antibiotics.
papers.abstract: Prolonged gestational antibiotic exposure was previously reported to impair EEG reactivity in adult offspring after perinatal asphyxia. It remained unclear to what extent the effect depended on perinatal insult. We assessed adult EEG reactivity after uncomplicated birth using the same gestational treatment paradigm. Pregnant Wistar rats received antibiotics (AB), probiotics (P), combined treatment (AB&P), or control (C). Adult offspring (AB: 5; P: 8; AB&P: 7; C: 9; 14 males) underwent intermittent photic stimulation during chloral-hydrate-induced EEG burst suppression. Reactivity to 60 s stimulation was quantified in 180 s trials using burst count reactivity (BCR) and the burst-suppression reactivity index (BSRi). After baseline burst count filtering, 200 trials were retained across groups. BCR did not differ significantly between groups. No multiplicity-corrected pairwise comparison identified a specific treatment-associated difference in BCR or BSRi. Mixed-effects models accounting for repeated trials likewise showed no significant overall group effect. Our small cohort did not provide evidence for a long-term effect of gestational antibiotic or probiotic exposure following uncomplicated birth. Together with the previous report, we suggest that gestational antibiotic administration could impair resilience to perinatal asphyxia at an exposure level without a readily detectable effect after uncomplicated birth.

papers.title: Large-Scale Neural Slowing Measured with Electroencephalography Indexes Secondary Thalamic Degeneration in Stroke.
papers.abstract: A central priority in stroke recovery research is the development of useful biomarkers that reveal underlying disease states to aid diagnosis, prognosis, stratification, and treatment, ideally using tools that are readily available in clinical settings. Large-scale neural slowing has the potential to be such a biomarker, but its usefulness is currently limited by uncertainty about its nature and relation to underlying pathophysiology. In this work, we sought to address these gaps by parameterizing abnormal resting-state electroencephalography spectral features across the scalp and investigating their relationship to thalamic atrophy and dysfunction, using structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a computational model of corticothalamic circuit dynamics, respectively. As predicted, stroke patients (n = 25; 15 males, 10 females) exhibited widespread spectral abnormalities, including significantly increased aperiodic exponent and offset, lower alpha frequency, and reduced beta power, which together can account for the frequently observed shift in power toward low frequencies after stroke. Furthermore, corticothalamic models fit to power spectral densities across the scalp inferred broad thalamic disinhibition. Crucially, these abnormalities (except beta reductions) were strongly associated with ipsilesional thalamic atrophy measured with MRI, despite the lack of direct thalamus damage in this sample. Overall, this work provides a deeper characterization of large-scale electrophysiological abnormalities after stroke and reinforces their potential as clinically feasible biomarkers of poststroke pathophysiology.

papers.title: The Orexinergic System in Alzheimer's Disease: From Sleep Disruption to Accelerated Neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake dysregulation is increasingly recognized as an early and clinically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), with growing evidence supporting a bidirectional relationship between disturbed sleep and AD pathophysiology. Sleep fragmentation and reduced slow-wave and REM sleep may contribute to amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation by increasing Aβ production during wakefulness and diminishing glymphatic clearance during sleep, while emerging amyloid pathology can further disrupt sleep architecture and circadian sleep-wake rhythm, reinforcing a feed-forward cycle. Within this framework, the orexinergic system, centered in the hypothalamus and crucial for arousal and sleep-wake stability, has been implicated as a mechanistic link between hyperarousal, impaired sleep consolidation, and altered amyloid dynamics. Preclinical studies suggested that orexin-A signaling can exacerbate Aβ and tau pathology and impair synaptic function, whereas biomarker studies reported high cerebrospinal fluid orexin-A levels in mild cognitive impairment and dementia due to AD. These observations raise the hypothesis that targeting orexin signaling and improving sleep may represent actionable strategies within the AD continuum. Clinical evidence indicates that behavioral and pharmacological interventions can improve sleep in at-risk populations, yet robust proof of disease-modifying effects on AD biomarkers or clinical progression remains limited. Ongoing trials of dual orexin receptor antagonists may clarify whether sustained modulation of sleep-wake regulation can influence AD-related biology beyond symptomatic sleep benefits.

papers.title: Effect of Intraindividual Variability in Sleep on Long-Term Memory Encoding in Sleep-Restricted Individuals.
papers.abstract: Greater variability in sleep across nights is generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, but some recent evidence suggests that for sleep-restricted individuals, a variable sleep schedule that allows for prophylactic and/or recovery sleep might lessen impairment in some basic cognitive functions compared to a stable schedule. This study examined whether multiple nights of sleep restriction with consistent or variable sleep duration affected declarative memory encoding differently. After two baseline nights of 8-h time-in-bed (TIB), 44 participants (21-26 years, 20 males) underwent five manipulation nights with one of three sleep schedules: 8-h TIB per night (control group), 6-h TIB per night (stable short sleep group) or 8-4-8-4-6 h TIB (variable short sleep group). A picture encoding task was administered after the fifth manipulation night, and memory performance was assessed in a recognition test after two recovery nights of 8-h TIB. Compared to the control group, the variable short sleep group exhibited poorer memory performance, characterised by a greater tendency towards 'unsure' responses for both old and new pictures (p = 0.05; p = 0.09). In contrast, the stable short sleep group did not show significant impairment in memory performance, but instead showed more correct rejections (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that among sleep-restricted individuals whose sleep duration varies substantially across nights, declarative memory may be encoded with reduced strength, thereby increasing response uncertainty at retrieval even after recovery sleep. Minimising sleep variability may optimise declarative memory encoding in sleep-restricted persons. Trial Registration: NCT04731662.

papers.title: Monitoring Reduced Vigilance Using an Eyeglass-Type EEG System.
papers.abstract: An eyeglass-type electroencephalography (EEG) device has emerged as a promising platform for continuous cognitive state monitoring owing to its seamless integration into daily life and greater usability compared with conventional headset-style EEG systems. However, the feasibility of EEG-based reduced-vigilance monitoring using this form factor remains insufficiently examined. To address this issue, we conducted a two-phase experiment involving 21 participants to establish a mental fatigue-sensitive index and validate a monitoring algorithm for reduced vigilance associated with drowsiness or mental fatigue using a custom-made eyeglass-type EEG device. In the first phase, a long-term sustained attention task (d2 test) was employed to induce mental fatigue, and the ratio of low-alpha to high-beta power was identified as a potential biomarker of mental-fatigue-related vigilance decline. In the second phase, system performance was evaluated through a prolonged, monotonous video-watching experiment designed to elicit reduced vigilance. The algorithm combined the drowsiness detection index (theta-plus-alpha power) from the TP9 and TP10 channels with the candidate fatigue-sensitive index from the differential channel. Subject-specific calibration-based thresholds were used to generate index-specific segment-level decisions, which were combined using a logical OR rule. In the pseudo-real-time evaluation of 16 participants, the final fusion model achieved a mean accuracy of 70.31%, a false-positive rate of 10.40%, a recall of 49.67%, and a precision of 81.80%, calculated from participant-level metrics. Detection performance depended partly on the inclusion of segments with prolonged eye closure, with lower recall after their exclusion. Nevertheless, these findings provide preliminary evidence for the feasibility of detecting behaviorally defined reduced vigilance using an eyeglass-type EEG device.

papers.title: Mitigating Sleep Inertia and Maintaining Neurobehavioral Performance in Shift Workers via Multisensory (Music and Light) Intervention: A Preliminary Field Study.
papers.abstract: Irregular shift schedules in railway operations increase safety risks through fatigue and sleep inertia. We evaluated a wearable multisensory device that delivers sleep-promoting music in darkness before sleep and uplifting music with blue light upon awakening. In a preliminary field crossover study, 17 railway staff completed the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), and Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) before and after on-duty sleep, with and without the device. In a separate electroencephalography (EEG) study, 10 healthy adults received sleep-onset and wake-up stimulation while EEG was recorded at Fz, Cz, and Pz. Compared to the control condition, the intervention maintained PVT response speed, reduced lapses at the end of the shift, and was associated with longer sleep duration. The PVT results, but not positive affect, remained significant after adjustment for pre-sleep values. Sleepiness was not significantly reduced overall and was lower only in an exploratory station subgroup. In the EEG study, the slow-to-fast power ratio increased during sleep-onset stimulation, and theta power was transiently lower early in wake-up stimulation than at the end of sleep-onset stimulation. These preliminary findings suggest that dual-phase multisensory stimulation may help sustain alertness in shift workers, although larger sham-controlled trials are needed.

papers.title: Peripheral sensory clocks drive nitroglycerin-induced rhythmic pain sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Mounting evidence has revealed circadian rhythms in pain sensitivity across multiple pain conditions, but the mechanisms that generate these rhythmic pain sensitivities remain unclear. We combined genetic models with tissue-specific knockout of the essential clock gene Bmal1 and a well-established nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced headache mouse model. Von Frey assays were performed to measure mechanical hypersensitivity at different times of the day. Circadian activity behavior, sleep and clock gene expression were also measured. Using trigeminal ganglion (TG) and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory neuron-specific Bmal1 knockout mice, we show that, in both male and female mice, loss of Bmal1 completely abolishes the diurnal rhythm of pain sensitivity but does not perturb basal nociception of NTG-induced hypersensitivity. In contrast, suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)-specific Bmal1 deletion in male mice eliminates circadian locomotor rhythms without altering rhythmic pain sensitivity, demonstrating that the central pacemaker SCN is not required for circadian rhythms of pain sensitivity. Dual deletion of Bmal1 in both SCN and sensory neurons replicates the sensory neuron-specific phenotype, confirming the dominant role of the peripheral sensory neuron clocks in male mice. Although sensory neuron Bmal1 loss alters sleep architecture, the free-running circadian period length remains intact. Together, these findings reveal that local molecular clocks in the peripheral nervous system drive diurnal rhythmicity of NTG-induced pain independently of the SCN.

papers.title: The EEG-Respiratory Gap: a deep learning biomarker associated with long-term mortality in obstructive sleep apnea
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) summarizes respiratory events by frequency, but was not designed to reflect how strongly an individual's brain responds to them. We developed a deep-learning model that estimates AHI from a single EEG channel (AHIbrain), developed using 22,044 polysomnography recordings and validated in an internal test set (r=0.88) and three external test sets (r=0.50-0.62). From AHIbrain, we derived two complementary metrics that characterize the EEG-Respiratory Gap: {Delta}AHIbrain, reflecting whether a patient's AHIbrain is higher or lower than expected for their measured AHI, and AHIbrain,event-free, estimated from epochs without scored respiratory events. Both were associated with sleep macro-, micro-, and epoch-level EEG features, suggesting that this discrepancy is not solely attributable to model error. Among participants free of cardiovascular disease, both metrics were associated with all-cause and non-CVD mortality after adjustment for AHI and clinical risk factors. After accounting for the same covariates, AHIbrain,event-free was also associated with CVD mortality in the highest-versus-lowest quartile comparison. These findings support the EEG-Respiratory Gap as an interpretable EEG-derived measure associated with prognostic information beyond AHI.

papers.title: Mapping global glymphatic system research (2012-2025): a scientometric and knowledge-mapping review integrating bioinformatics perspectives on aging.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is a newly discovered brain-wide clearance pathway offering promising novel therapeutic interventions across diverse medical conditions. Accordingly, a comprehensive overview mapping scientific knowledge is currently urgent. Our study examined the spatiotemporal evolution of research output, institutions, authors, journals, as well as their mutual interactions. With publications steadily increasing, the field has shifted from animal studies toward human research, and demonstrated an evolutionary trajectory from fundamental mechanisms to advancing clinical applications. Keywords analysis identified five thematic clusters covering disease associations, system dynamics and drug delivery, sleep and aging-related clearance, neuroimaging, and cognitive impairment including Alzheimer's disease. Analysis of GEO datasets identified aging and glymphatic related genes converging on PI3K-Akt and FoxO signaling, central regulators of survival, stress responses, and longevity. Our findings highlight the need for approaches capable of quantifying perivascular fluid transport and glial-vascular interactions, especially in the context of aging-related structural change. Such cross-disciplinary convergence is essential for translating mechanistic insights into clinically actionable, glymphatic-targeted interventions that may have promising potential for various brain disorders.

papers.title: Lactobacillus Fermentation-Derived γ-Aminobutyric Acid Improves Sleep Parameters in Invertebrate and Vertebrate Models.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the sleep-promoting effects of Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) produced by Lactobacillus fermentation using invertebrate and vertebral models. The activity of GABA derived from lactic acid bacteria (GABArelax®) was analyzed through subjective day-night movement and sleep-related parameters in fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) and sleep duration, neurotransmitter-related factors, and brain waves in ICR mice and SD-rats. In Drosophila, GABArelax® increased total sleep time and reduced nighttime and daytime locomotor activity, with the 3% treatment producing effects comparable to those of benzodiazepine. Video-tracking analysis further demonstrated that 2% and 3% GABArelax® reduced the total distance traveled, locomotor velocity, and overall mobility, while exerting relatively limited effects on the total duration of active and inactive behavior. In ICR mice, GABArelax® increased the mRNA expression of GABAergic and serotonergic receptors, including GABAA-R, GABAB-R1, GABAB-R2, and Htr1a. These transcriptional changes were accompanied by elevated brain concentrations of GABA and 5-hydroxytryptamine and enhanced expression of antioxidant defense-related genes, including SOD, Gpx1, and CAT. Electroencephalographic analysis in SD-rats showed that GABArelax® reduced wakefulness and prolonged total sleep duration. This increase was predominantly attributable to an extension of non-rapid eye movement sleep, whereas high-dose administration reduced REM sleep and enhanced δ-wave activity, an electrophysiological marker of deep sleep. Overall, these findings demonstrate that GABArelax® promotes sleep through coordinated regulation of GABAergic and serotonergic neurotransmission, reinforcement of antioxidant defense, and improvement of sleep architecture. GABArelax® therefore represents a promising food-derived functional ingredient for the management of sleep disturbances and the improvement of sleep quality.

papers.title: Beyond dream enactment: Pharmacological effects on REM atonia in REM sleep behavior disorder - a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Pharmacological treatments for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) aim to reduce injurious dream enactment, but their effects on the underlying loss of REM atonia remain uncertain. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, CENTRAL, and trial registries through October 15, 2026 for studies reporting quantitative REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) during pharmacological treatment of adults with isolated RBD or RBD associated with a clinically manifest synucleinopathy. Screening and methodological assessments were reconciled by two reviewers. Risk of bias and certainty were evaluated using design-appropriate tools. Findings were synthesized by drug and RSWA component without meta-analysis because comparable effect estimates were insufficient. Seventeen reports representing 16 independent studies were included: three randomized trials, 11 nonrandomized longitudinal studies, and two cross-sectional studies. Clonazepam was associated with variable changes in phasic and tonic EMG activity, without conclusive evidence of consistent improvement in quantitative REM atonia. Melatonin studies suggested possible improvements in some RSWA measures, whereas dopaminergic treatment frequently improved clinical symptoms without significant RSWA change. No randomized comparison demonstrated clear superiority for quantitative RSWA. Small samples, heterogeneous scoring, and incomplete comparative data limited certainty. Current evidence does not establish consistent pharmacological improvement in quantitative REM atonia in RBD, despite frequently reported symptomatic benefits. This does not demonstrate the absence of physiological drug effects, given the limited precision, methodological heterogeneity, and variable emphasis placed on RSWA across studies. Clinical improvement and quantitative REM atonia should therefore remain distinct but complementary outcomes in future trials, including investigations of potential neuroprotective treatments.

papers.title: Integrating bioethnography into sleep research: generating better measures, hypotheses, and interpretations.
papers.abstract: Sleep research increasingly uses actigraphy, biomarkers, and structured surveys to quantify sleep duration and quality across populations. Yet researchers often interpret these measures without sufficient attention to the social, relational, and structural contexts surrounding sleep. This report presents bioethnography as a complementary methodological approach integrating sustained ethnographic engagement with epidemiological research. The report situates bioethnography alongside developmental-cultural, social-ecological, biocultural, and clinically oriented ecological approaches to sleep and identifies bioethnography's specific contribution: an iterative research architecture allowing ethnographic findings to reshape hypotheses, measurements, analyses, and interpretations of biological data. Drawing on a bioethnographic study of sleep among midlife women enrolled in a long-standing cohort in Mexico City, the report demonstrates how open-ended inquiry generates new hypotheses, reveals unmeasured social processes shaping sleep, and refines the interpretation of quantitative sleep metrics. By situating biological data within lived experience, bioethnography produces 'better numbers': more valid, interpretable findings responsive to population-specific realities. The report discusses the approach's strengths and limitations and outlines practical strategies for integrating bioethnography into sleep research. Bioethnography does not replace established ecological or biosocial frameworks; rather, the approach offers a way to operationalize a shared commitment to understanding sleep as a biological process embedded in social life.

papers.title: Single- and Multi-SNP Genotype Analyses of the Circadian-Related SLC20A2 Gene Reveal Sex-Specific Associations with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD).
papers.abstract: Circadian clock gene variants have been linked to mood disorders, including seasonal affective disorder (SAD), suggesting that molecular pathways affecting seasonal mood are influenced by the circadian clock and sleep-wake patterns, but the molecular mechanisms underlying these links are poorly understood. Building on animal and human evidence that SLC20A2 influences seasonal circadian adaptation, we tested associations between five SLC20A2 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and symptoms of SAD and depression. We examined both single-SNP and multi-SNP genotypes in a deeply phenotyped undergraduate population and assessed whether these associations differed by sex. Seasonality scores were strongly associated with differences in seasonal sleep duration in this population. Three SNPs (rs6988483, rs13281070, rs3763510) were significantly associated with self-reported SAD symptom severity, with the effects of SLC-3 and SLC-4 concentrated in males. Multi-SNP genotype analysis identified eight multi-SNP combinations associated with self-reported SAD. One risk genotype conferred roughly nine times greater odds of SAD symptoms in females, and this genotype and two protective genotypes showed no corresponding association with general depressive symptoms, suggesting these variants influence seasonal depression specifically, rather than depressive symptoms broadly. Five additional genotypes were protective against both SAD and depression. These findings provide initial evidence that SLC20A2 variation, at both the single-SNP and genotype level, may contribute to SAD risk in a sex-specific manner and that a subset of this variation may act on seasonal mood regulation independent of general depression risk. Our results support SLC20A2 as a candidate gene for circadian-related mood disorders and point to potential new therapeutic targets, though replication in larger, sex-balanced cohorts is needed.

papers.title: Diurnal Variation in Human Breast Milk: Multi-Omic Characterization and Implications for Infant Circadian Development.
papers.abstract: Components of human breast milk exhibit circadian rhythms that may convey maternal chronobiological signals to infants; however, the diurnal patterns of the milk microbiome and metabolome remain poorly characterized. A cross-sectional study was conducted to assess feeding practices and neonatal sleep patterns in 89 mother-infant dyads. Additionally, 40 breast milk samples were collected from 20 lactating women in a separate cohort at both noon and midnight. Melatonin was measured in all 40 milk samples, microbial composition and metabolites in 13 pairs samples were quantified by LC-MS and metagenomic sequencing. In univariate analysis, neonates receiving mixed feeding demonstrated shorter nocturnal sleep compared to those exclusively breastfed; however, these associations were no longer significant after adjustment for delivery mode. A total of 335,651 microbial features were shared between the noon and midnight samples. Differential abundance analysis identified 20 bacterial genera that differed significantly between the two sampling times. The midnight samples exhibited higher relative abundances of Cognataquiflexum, Segnochrobactrum, and Aquabacterium, with both time points enriched in pathways related to lipid and amino acid metabolism. The noon-midnight differences observed suggest potential implications for infant circadian development. The potential role of circadian-matched breastfeeding strategies in infant development requires further investigation.

papers.title: Shared sleep fragmentation in undergraduate roommates: dyadic actigraphy in a dense urban campus setting.
papers.abstract: Dyadic sleep research has focused on romantic partners, leaving open whether nonromantic people who share a sleep space show related sleep. We examined sleep continuity and roommate concordance among undergraduate roommate dyads on a dense urban campus bordered by an interstate highway, freight-rail corridors, and an overnight air-cargo hub. The setting is described as context; no environmental exposure was measured. Baseline data were analyzed from 29 roommate dyads (58 participants aged 18-19 years) enrolling in a mindfulness program at the University of Louisville in 2017. Participants were instructed to wear wrist actigraphs for four nights and completed one-week versions of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and Perceived Stress Scale. The planned analysis estimated roommate concordance with intraclass correlations (ICC); analyses of same-night covariation, bedroom sharing, and perceived stress were exploratory. To separate roommate similarity from shared calendar timing, roommates were compared with same-wave non-roommates (pseudo-dyads), and night-level analyses were adjusted for day of week and week of semester. Participants averaged 6.98 h of sleep, 66 min of wake after sleep onset (WASO), and 18.6 actigraphy-detected awakenings per night. Roommate concordance was clearest for awakening frequency (ICC = 0.38, 95% CI [0.04, 0.68]), which exceeded pseudo-dyad concordance (mean ICC = 0.09); after centering on data-collection wave it was lower and imprecise (ICC = 0.25 [-0.11, 0.59]). Six other actigraphy outcomes had smaller estimates, with intervals including zero. Roommates' night-to-night deviations in WASO were correlated (r = 0.29 [0.07, 0.44]); this association persisted after day-of-week and week-of-semester adjustment and exceeded 95% of pseudo-dyad re-pairings, whereas same-night covariation in awakenings did not. Bedroom-sharing comparisons (18 vs. 10 dyads) were too imprecise to be informative. Perceived stress was associated with participants' own PSQI scores (β = 0.55 [0.39, 0.71]) and, more weakly, their own WASO (β = 0.23 [0.04, 0.43]). Undergraduate roommates showed modest similarity in sleep fragmentation that was not fully explained by shared calendar timing, extending dyadic sleep research beyond romantic partners. Because environmental exposures were not measured, the findings cannot be attributed to the urban setting; studies pairing dyadic sleep measurement with synchronized environmental monitoring are needed.

papers.title: Impact of Ambient Temperature on PAP Adherence: A Retrospective Analysis of a Prospective OSA Cohort.
papers.abstract: Early adherence failure is a major driver of positive airway pressure (PAP) discontinuation in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Although seasonal variation in PAP use has been reported, the relationship between environmental conditions at treatment initiation and clinically defined early adherence remains incompletely understood. This study evaluated whether ambient temperature at PAP initiation was associated with subsequent PAP adherence and compared its relative contribution with conventional baseline clinical factors. This retrospective analysis used a prospectively enrolled OSA cohort. Overall, 342 adults who initiated auto-adjusting PAP therapy between 2018 and 2024 were included. Adherence was defined according to Korean national insurance criteria as PAP use for ≥4 hours per night on ≥70% of nights during any consecutive 28-day period within the first 3 months. Ambient temperature at PAP initiation was obtained from national meteorological data. Hierarchical logistic regression was performed using variables available at or before PAP initiation. A logistic regression-based SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework with repeated stratified cross-validation was used to compare relative feature contributions, and a feature-ablation analysis was used to evaluate the contributions of temperature and baseline AHI to model discrimination. Among 342 patients, 238 (69.6%) met adherence criteria. Adherence was lower in patients initiating PAP during May-September than during October- April (61.7% vs. 75.1%, P=0.008). In the fully adjusted baseline model (n=334), higher monthly mean daily maximum temperature was associated with lower odds of adherence (OR, 0.95 per 1°C increase; 95% CI, 0.92- 0.98; P=0.001). Higher temperature was also associated with shorter average daily PAP use at 3 months in a secondary analysis. The crossvalidated logistic model showed modest discrimination (AUROC, 0.653± 0.059). Within this model, temperature showed the largest mean absolute SHAP value, followed by baseline AHI. Excluding temperature or baseline AHI reduced the AUROC to a similar extent (0.029 for both), indicating comparable contributions to discrimination. Higher ambient temperature at PAP initiation was associated with lower early PAP adherence and contributed to model discrimination to a degree comparable to that of baseline OSA severity. Patients initiating PAP during warmer periods, particularly summer, may warrant closer early follow-up and additional support to facilitate PAP adaptation and adherence.

papers.title: Impaired corneal nerve repair and regeneration after injury in mouse sleep deprivation model.
papers.abstract: To investigate the impact of sleep deprivation (SD) on corneal nerve repair and regeneration following injury and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms. Female C57BL/6 mice, aged 10-12wk, were allocated to either the SD group or the normal control (NC) group based on sleep duration. A corneal injury model was established to evaluate the rate of corneal epithelial healing and the dynamics of wound repair. Immunofluorescence staining assessed changes in corneal basal nerve fiber density. Corneal sensitivity was measured using the Cochet-Bonnet esthesiometer. A quantitative polymerase chain reaction was conducted to determine changes in the expression of nerve growth factor (NGF) in mouse corneal tissues. Furthermore, RNA-sequencing was performed for in-depth analysis of the corneal transcriptome following epithelial injury. On day 6 post-injury, the SD group exhibited significantly lower central and peripheral corneal nerve fiber density compared with the NC group. Corneal sensitivity in the SD group was substantially lower than in the NC group. NGF expression in the cornea was significantly lower in the SD group compared with the NC group. Additionally, the corneal transcriptome of the SD group exhibited significant alterations compared to the NC group, notably a downregulation of nerve-related gene expression following SD treatment. Pathway analysis further revealed that SD inhibited multiple pathways associated with nerve repair. These findings demonstrate that SD significantly delays repair and regeneration following corneal nerve injury, providing novel theoretical perspectives into its detrimental effect on ocular health.

papers.title: Sea-Level Polysomnography and Periodic Breathing During Acute Normobaric Hypoxia in Healthy Adults: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Acute exposure to high altitude without prior acclimatization can induce periodic breathing (PB) in healthy individuals, but practical methods for identifying susceptibility before ascent are lacking. This exploratory study examined whether sea-level polysomnography (PSG) findings were associated with PB during acute normobaric hypoxia in healthy individuals. Fifty-four healthy young adults underwent full PSG at sea level and again under normobaric hypoxia after the chamber was set to a nominal simulated altitude of 3500 m; the device-reported oxygen fraction was 13.49% (approximately equivalent to 3300-3350 m under standard-atmosphere oxygen partial-pressure matching). According to hypoxic PSG findings, participants were classified as non-sleep-disordered breathing (non-SDB), SDB without PB, or SDB with PB. Sea-level PSG variables were then compared among groups. During acute normobaric hypoxia, 20 participants remained in the non-SDB group, 23 developed SDB without PB, and 11 developed SDB with PB. At sea level, the oxygen desaturation index (ODI), apnea-hypopnea index, non-rapid eye movement apnea-hypopnea index, average oxygen saturation during non-rapid eye movement sleep, and lowest oxygen saturation differed significantly among groups. In multivariable analysis, sea-level ODI was independently associated with PB during hypoxia. Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that sea-level ODI had moderate discriminatory ability for PB, with an area under the curve of 0.798 (stratified-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 0.653-0.920; DeLong P<0.001). At a cutoff of 1.15 events/h, sensitivity was 81.8% and specificity was 79.1%. In this exploratory study, sea-level ODI was associated with PB during acute normobaric hypoxia and may help identify individuals susceptible to hypoxia-related PB. Validation in larger, more sex-balanced cohorts is needed.

papers.title: Plasma Metabolic Proteomics Links Phenoconversion and Disease-Specific Brain 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Pattern Expressions in Isolated REM Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: Cellular metabolic dysfunction has emerged as a key contributor to neurodegeneration, but its role in Lewy body disease (LBD), particularly during prodromal stages, remains unclear. We investigated targeted blood-based proteomic profiles related to metabolic pathways across the REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-LBD continuum, and explored their potential as biomarkers of disease severity and phenoconversion. In this prospective cohort study, we enrolled 116 patients across the RBD-LBD continuum, including 47 with polysomnography-confirmed isolated RBD (iRBD), 45 with Parkinson's disease (PD) with RBD, and 24 with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) with RBD, along with 30 age-matched healthy controls. Plasma concentrations of 92 metabolism-related proteins were measured using a proximity extension assay. Motor function, neuropsychological assessments, and brain 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging were obtained. Patients with iRBD were prospectively followed for up to 4 years to monitor phenoconversion. Compared with controls, 16 differentially expressed metabolism-related proteins were identified across the RBD-LBD continuum, with predominant enrichment in neutrophil degranulation pathways. These protein alterations were mainly observed in patients with clinically manifest LBD, with DOPA decarboxylase demonstrating the most prominent differential expression and significant correlations with levodopa equivalent daily dose. In contrast, only N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was significantly upregulated in patients with iRBD. Elevated NT-proBNP levels were associated with orthostatic intolerance, increased PD- and DLB-related metabolic brain pattern expressions, and earlier phenoconversion. Plasma metabolic proteins showed stage-specific alterations across the RBD-LBD continuum. NT-proBNP may have potential as a marker of short-term phenoconversion risk in iRBD. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in central vestibular compensation and in the pathogenesis of vestibular disorders: preclinical evidence, mechanistic bridges, and a causal research agenda.
papers.abstract: Recovery from acute vestibular damage depends on central compensation (plasticity within the vestibular nuclei) rather than on repair of the peripheral lesion. The cellular mechanisms of compensation have classically been framed in neuronal terms; over the past two decades, evidence has accumulated that glial and inflammatory processes participate in the course of compensation and can be manipulated to alter it. To map the evidence for neuroinflammation in central vestibular compensation with explicit attention to its strength, directness, and boundaries, and to derive a falsifiable mechanistic framework and research agenda. Structured PubMed search ([tiab]-restricted queries; 71 unique records screened, 69 on 2 September 2026 and 2 on a 25 October 2026 re-run; 37 included, graded A-E and by directness), supplemented by contextual pools and classic reference studies. Narrative synthesis; not a systematic review. Direct evidence is confined to 20 original preclinical studies that measured glial or inflammatory processes in vestibular models: 14 used injury or overload paradigms, in which the question is compensation, and 6 used disease models, which address pathogenesis rather than compensation. In the injury and overload paradigms, glial responses accompany deafferentation and sustained vestibular stimulation; suppressing acute inflammation (methylprednisolone), exacerbating it (LPS), or sustaining it (sleep deprivation through TLR4/NF-κB/NLRP3) all impair compensation, while interventions that alter glial abundance or marker-defined state are associated with improved recovery. In vestibular migraine and ischemic vertigo models, inflammatory pathways contribute to central sensitization. Human brain evidence identified by our structured PubMed search was limited to one TSPO-PET study in vestibular schwannoma; the search identified no direct vestibular-nucleus glial evidence in primary vestibular disorders. We propose a dual-phase, state-dependent glial hypothesis: a supportive acute window whose inflammatory level must remain "homeostatic," followed by a decompensation risk if inflammation persists or polarizes, with a separate, hypothesis-level inflammation-to-sensitization path for vestibular migraine and PPPD. Priority experiments are time-windowed cell-type-specific manipulations in models and TSPO-PET of the vestibular nuclei in acute vestibular neuritis and PPPD. Neuroinflammation is currently best regarded as a candidate modulator of vestibular compensation requiring causal validation, not an established disease mechanism.

papers.title: Condition-associated EEG signatures in N-back tasks: temporal dynamics, classification, and generalization.
papers.abstract: Mental workload (MWL) monitoring with electroencephalography (EEG) is promising for adaptive systems, but practical use requires models that remain reliable across time, tasks, and users with feasible sensor layouts. This study investigated condition-associated EEG signatures in 15 healthy adults performing two complementary N-back paradigms: an N-back level manipulation (N-LEVELS: 1-back, 2-back, 3-back) and a stimulus-pacing manipulation at fixed 2-back (N-SPEED: slow, medium, fast). EEG was recorded using a compact 8-channel setup. Spectral bandpower features, composite workload indices, and N2/P3b ERP markers were analyzed. Linear classifiers were evaluated using within-subject TRAIN → TEST and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols, together with analyses of observation duration, time-on-task dynamics, temporal generalization, cross-paradigm transfer, and exploratory ordinal regression. N-LEVELS and N-SPEED produced distinct behavioral and subjective profiles: increasing N-back level was associated with greater task demand, whereas faster N-SPEED conditions showed greater perceived temporal demand and reduced response-time availability. Exploratory locally corrected spectral analyses suggested more frequent beta-band and engagement-index modulation in N-LEVELS and more frequent posterior/parietal alpha suppression and theta/alpha-related modulation in N-SPEED. ERP analyses showed reduced P3b amplitude under higher N-back levels and faster pacing. Classification performance was modest and context-dependent: N-SPEED three-class decoding was more consistent than N-LEVELS, and all three N-SPEED pairwise contrasts survived correction under both WITHIN and LOSO evaluation, whereas in N-LEVELS only the 1-back vs. 3-back contrast survived under LOSO. Post hoc artifact-sensitivity analyses supported the principal P3b findings and largely preserved reference-decoding and alpha time-on-task patterns. After delta-band removal, neither three-class LOSO result nor the N-SPEED slow-vs.-medium and medium-vs.-fast LOSO contrasts survived correction; N-SPEED slow vs. medium under LOSO also did not survive either high-pass variant. Exploratory ordinal regression showed a clearer ordered relationship for N-SPEED than N-LEVELS. Time-on-task analyses revealed selective non-stationarity, mainly progressive alpha build-up, whereas cross-paradigm transfer did not survive corrected inference. These findings indicate that compact EEG recordings contain condition-associated information, but the small sample, deterministic block order, modest decoding performance, and limited cross-paradigm generalization constrain causal attribution and applicability beyond the present protocol.

papers.title: AI-assisted development of a rule-based pipeline for pre-examination screening in clinical neuropsychology: An exploratory method-development study.
papers.abstract: We present an exploratory, method-development study of a framework for rule-based pre-examination screening. The study is exploratory: no clinical endpoint, success threshold, or control condition was pre-specified. Demonstrated on retrospectively analyzed irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) data, the pipeline produces a structured analysis with cross-domain pattern detection and audience-tailored reports. A large language model was used as a coding assistant to draft scoring logic, cross-domain rules, and Python code. The deployed pipeline executes these fixed rules deterministically; no model inference occurs when patient data are processed. The pipeline processes five instruments (Bergen Insomnia Scale, Conners' Continuous Performance Test, Chalder Fatigue Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status). For each patient, it generates an eight-step processing sequence, visualizations, and clinician-gated reports. Analyses used data from 105 adults (65 IBS, 40 controls) from the Bergen Brain-Gut-Microbiota study. The tool flagged findings above threshold in sleep (50%), fatigue (40%), anxiety (35%), and attention (30%), with multi-domain flags in 60%. Cross-domain rules linked co-occurring findings to candidate mechanisms drawn from published literature. Two case illustrations demonstrated the rule-based summaries alongside clinician interpretation that went beyond the rules. The framework is a transparent support tool rather than an autonomous reasoning system: every output traces to a stated rule, and the contribution of artificial intelligence lies in development, not deployment: it augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Because the analysis is exploratory and single-cohort, the findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective, comparative validation.

papers.title: Natural Antioxidants in Sleep Deprivation: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Potential, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Sleep Deprivation (SD) is a condition that undermines the body's functional state and is associated with impaired cognition and immunity, dysfunction of the circulatory and metabolic systems, and circadian misalignment. These alterations are accompanied by biologic stress, neuroendocrine imbalance, oxidative stress, and inflammation, affecting both the central nervous system and peripheral organs. Owing to this dual inflammatory and oxidative nature, antioxidant-based interventions have emerged as promising complementary therapeutic approaches. This review summarizes and critically discusses the current evidence on naturally occurring antioxidant compounds and plant extracts with potential protective effects against SD-related pathophysiological alterations, with emphasis on their molecular mechanisms of action and their multifunctional pharmacological properties. Particular attention is given to their antioxidant, antiinflammatory, hypolipidemic, antidiabetic, and cytoprotective activities, as well as their ability to modulate oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling associated with SD. Overall, the available evidence suggests that natural antioxidants may attenuate the deleterious consequences of SD through pleiotropic mechanisms. However, further mechanistic studies and well-designed clinical investigations are required to establish their therapeutic value. In addition to their potential clinical applications, these compounds may provide further insight into the molecular pathways underlying SD pathology and facilitate the development of novel natural therapeutic agents.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Insights to Rational Interventions in Parkinson's Disease: An Integrated Approach with a Patient Perspective.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the selective loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, accompanied by the accumulation and spreading of misfolded α-synuclein aggregates. Proposed mechanisms relevant to PD include gut-brain propagation of pathology via autonomic circuits, autophagy-related maintenance of proteostasis, and sleep-associated glymphatic clearance of extracellular waste. These mechanisms have prompted interest in multimodal approaches targeting disease-relevant biological pathways. Whether such approaches modify the neurodegenerative process or predominantly promote functional adaptation and compensation remains an open question. Methods: In a real-world clinical setting, a single patient with early-stage PD was observed over two years while five interventions targeting disease-relevant pathways were introduced at different time points and partly overlapped. Evaluation included physician-based clinical assessments and patient-reported observations, complemented by wearable-derived monitoring of autonomic and sleep metrics during the final six months. Serial DAT-SPECT imaging at baseline and two-year follow-up assessed changes in DAT binding. Results: Motor impairment remained mild and the patient reported largely stable overall mobility, although the persistent unilateral tremor was perceived to increase gradually later in the observation period. During the final six months, wearable monitoring indicated relative stable nocturnal autonomic measures and no markedly atypical rapid eye movement (REM) sleep estimates, while suggesting reduced slow-wave sleep (SWS). Following implementation of a structured bedtime routine, wearable-derived SWS estimates increased. Serial DAT-SPECT imaging demonstrated lower striatal DAT binding at two-year follow-up despite clinical stability. Conclusions: In this individual case, relative clinical stability coexisted with a longitudinal reduction in striatal DAT binding. Although no inference regarding disease modification can be drawn from a single uncontrolled observation, this discordance illustrates the limitations of interpreting clinical stability alone as evidence of an unchanged underlying disease process.

papers.title: PFedHASNet: A Personalized Federated Hybrid Analog-Spike Network for Multi-Subject Motor Imagery EEG Decoding
papers.abstract: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) data are often collected and stored separately across subjects or institutions, and EEG acquisition and annotation remain costly. Training models solely on individual subject data limits the use of information from other subjects, whereas centralizing raw EEG recordings raises privacy and data governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw EEG data, providing a practical approach to leveraging information from multiple subjects. Accordingly, we propose PFedHASNet, a personalized federated hybrid analog-spike network for MI-EEG decoding. The shared encoder integrates continuous-valued temporal features, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spike responses, and channel-wise log-variance statistics through learnable fusion weights. Client-private residual adapters and classifiers perform subject-specific feature refinement and personalized prediction, respectively. Experiments on held-out trials from participating subjects across four public MI-EEG datasets show that PFedHASNet achieves the highest mean client macro-F1 among 18 model configurations in cross-model comparisons, while maintaining competitive decoding performance with a compact client-side model in comparisons using the same backbone. Ablation studies further examine the contributions of hybrid representations and personalization components to decoding performance.

papers.title: Integrating Inflammation, Pathway Modulation, and Circadian Clock Genes: Conventional and Phytochemical Strategies for Safer Osteoporosis Therapy.
papers.abstract: Osteoporosis is a systemic and silent bone disease that destroys bone microarchitecture, thereby increasing the risk of bone fracture, leading to increased morbidity and mortality. Although it is usually considered a structural deficit, bone remodeling is now fundamentally dependent on the circadian clock, osteoblast cells (responsible for the formation of new bone tissues), osteoclast cells (responsible for breaking down bone tissues), and hormonal rhythms, such as cortisol, melatonin, growth hormone, and parathyroid hormones. Current treatment methods for osteoporosis do not fully restore bone quality and cause many side effects. To address these problems, recent studies have suggested that phytomolecules, as promising therapeutic candidates, can be used for treatment. The use of phytomolecules in combination with conventional treatment, in a time-sensitive manner aligned with circadian biology, is expected to be a better treatment for osteoporosis. Disturbances in the sleep-wake cycle or in neurotransmitter homeostasis dysregulate core clock genes (BMAL-1, CLOCK, PER, CRY) in bone cells, causing instability in bone turnover. Osteochronotherapy involves scheduling the intake of conventional drugs and phytochemicals in accordance with the circadian rhythms of bone cells. This chronobiological method aims to achieve the highest therapeutic efficacy and the lowest toxicity, representing an advanced approach to osteoporosis treatment. In vitro studies have shown that bioactive agents, mainly resveratrol, icariin, genistein, quercetin, and baicalein, have osteoprotective activities with multimodal actions, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct effects on RANKL/OPG, AMPK/SIRT1, ESR, NF-κB, and Wnt/β-catenin. The study highlights the importance of incorporating circadian biology into osteoporosis management. The synchronization of therapies with the biological clock can maximize efficiency, reduce adverse effects, and help develop a new approach to bone health. The results emphasize the importance of using phytochemicals as an adjunct therapy, shed light on knowledge gaps in bone remodeling, and suggest possible avenues for utilizing circadian regulation of osteoblasts and osteoclasts to enhance bone density. Furthermore, the incorporation of natural compounds with chronotherapy represents a paradigm shift toward more personalized, safer, and biologically harmonized strategies for osteoporosis therapy. These insights also highlight critical knowledge gaps in bone remodeling research, encouraging future studies to explore how circadian rhythms and neurotransmitter pathways can be leveraged to advance precision medicine in skeletal health. It is now evident that circadian rhythm serves as an important mediator for the maintenance of healthy bones because of its function in bone remodeling. In future research, emphasis must also be placed on exploring the possible differential regulation of osteoclasts and osteoblasts by various circadian rhythms and how such regulation can help enhance bone strength. The review concludes by examining the interplay among neurotransmitter pathways, circadian biology, and sleep quality in relation to conventional and phytochemical interventions.

papers.title: Multi-scale feature fusion and neural architecture search for electroencephalography-based affective-state recognition in public benchmark datasets.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG)-based affective-state recognition may provide an objective neurophysiological complement to self-report scales and behavioral observations, but robust modeling remains difficult because EEG signals are non-stationary, temporally heterogeneous, and strongly subject-dependent. This study evaluated MFANet, a multi-scale feature fusion and neural architecture search-enhanced framework for binary classification of valence, arousal, and dominance. MFANet combines parallel one-dimensional convolutional branches with different receptive fields, channel-wise attention for adaptive feature recalibration, and a neural architecture search-guided long short-term memory module for temporal modeling. The framework was evaluated on the public DEAP and DREAMER datasets using five-fold, trial-grouped subject-dependent cross-validation in which all windows from one stimulus trial remained in the same outer fold and all data-dependent operations were confined to the corresponding training data. In DEAP ablation experiments, the complete model achieved mean accuracies of 97.20 ± 1.63% for valence, 97.32 ± 1.27% for arousal, and 97.14 ± 1.21% for dominance. Compared with the basic convolutional-recurrent baseline, multi-scale feature fusion and the searched recurrent module improved average accuracy by 10.17 and 10.87 percentage points, respectively, corresponding to relative gains of 12.5% and 13.4%. In participant-level paired comparisons based on the archived participant-level values, MFANet exceeded the dynamic graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) by 4.13, 3.39, and 3.71 percentage points; bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were 3.29-5.15, 2.56-4.38, and 2.74-4.85, and all Holm-adjusted p-values were <0.001. A DEAP channel-count sensitivity analysis indicated that the full 32-channel montage changed accuracy by less than 0.4 percentage points relative to the prespecified 14-channel montage. These findings suggest that joint multi-scale representation learning and adaptive recurrent architecture selection can improve benchmark EEG affective-state recognition. Because the analysis used public healthy-volunteer datasets and self-reported affective labels, the framework should be regarded as a computational method for future clinical validation rather than a diagnostic tool.

papers.title: Footwear-Related Modulation of Scalp EEG Theta/Alpha Ratio During Walking in Children: An Exploratory Within-Subject Study.
papers.abstract: Background: Childhood is a critical period for neuromotor development, during which footwear may influence the sensory and mechanical context of walking. This study examined whether footwear condition was associated with changes in scalp-level EEG activity during walking in 37 typically developing children aged 6-7 years. Methods: Participants completed repeated 10 m walking trials under three randomized conditions: barefoot, barefoot-style footwear, and conventional structured footwear. EEG was recorded using a mobile 14-channel Emotiv EPOC X system. The primary outcome was the global Theta/Alpha ratio averaged across scalp electrodes. Results: Footwear condition significantly affected the global Theta/Alpha ratio (F (2,72) = 14.57, p < 0.001). Conventional structured footwear produced higher Theta/Alpha values than both barefoot walking and barefoot-style footwear, whereas no significant differences were found between barefoot and barefoot-style conditions. Mean paired differences were 1.08 for conventional versus barefoot and 0.99 for conventional versus barefoot-style footwear. Similar directional effects were observed across electrode groupings. No significant differences were identified in absolute theta, alpha, or beta power, global Beta/Alpha ratio, or Shannon entropy. Conclusions: Conventional structured footwear was associated with increased scalp-level Theta/Alpha activity during walking in children, suggesting possible footwear-related modulation of attentional or motor-control demands.

papers.title: Process, Heterogeneity, and Modifiable Risk Factors of Postoperative Recovery After Cardiac Surgery.
papers.abstract: Cardiac surgery improves clinical endpoints but imposes challenges in recovery. Understanding patient-reported postoperative recovery is crucial for optimal care. The goal of this study was to reveal the process, heterogeneity, and modifiable risk factors of patient-reported postoperative recovery. In this multicenter prospective cohort study involving patients undergoing nonemergent cardiac surgery, patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the Fuwai-Cardiac Recovery Scale (a 9-item scale including symptoms and functional status) at baseline and 8 timepoints after surgery (days 1-4, weeks 2 and 3, and months 1 and 3). Total score and each item score of the Fuwai-Cardiac Recovery Scale were reported to characterize the recovery process. Group-based trajectory models were applied to detect heterogeneity, and trajectory with the largest area under trajectory curve was defined as poor recovery pattern. Multivariable stepwise regression was performed to uncover modifiable risk factors of poor recovery. From May 2023 to December 2024, 2,993 patients from 8 Chinese centers were enrolled. The proportions of patients achieving a total score ≤30 (less likely to experience 3-month unplanned readmission) were 77.4% at discharge (week 2) and 97.7% at month 3. Areas under the curve of the item score within 2 weeks, ranked from highest to lowest, were thirst, toileting dependency, poor mobility, fatigue, pain, poor sleep, poor appetite, shortness of breath, and nausea or vomiting. Three different poor recovery patterns were identified: 1) "initial worsening followed by improving" in shortness of breath, poor appetite, nausea or vomiting, poor sleep, and pain; 2) "persistently not improving" in thirst; and 3) "slowly improving" in fatigue, poor mobility, and toileting dependency. Several modifiable risk factors were significantly associated with poor recovery patterns, including smoking (shortness of breath, OR: 1.55; 95% CI: 1.07-2.24), obesity (poor mobility, OR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.02-2.26), and anemia (poor appetite, OR: 1.47; 95% CI: 1.11-1.95; fatigue, OR: 1.36; 95% CI: 1.11-1.67). Recovery after cardiac surgery is a dynamic trajectory that unfolds over time, differs substantially among patients, and offers opportunities for earlier recognition and intervention.

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in Experienced Dancers: A Virtual Reality Comparative Analysis.
papers.abstract: Dance is a complex activity that integrates motor, sensory, and cognitive processes and requires rapid responses, attentional control, and precise sensorimotor integration. Virtual reality (VR) may provide an immersive approach for assessing cognitive performance in contexts relevant to dance. This study aimed to compare reaction time (RT), decision time (DT), attention (AT), and inhibitory control (IC) between experienced dancers and non-dancers using an immersive VR assessment. This cross-sectional study included 26 participants: 13 experienced dancers (9 women, 4 men; 22.15 ± 3.69 years) and 13 non-dancers (9 women, 4 men; 24.15 ± 2.85 years). Cognitive performance was assessed using the NeuroSport Arena VR system, which included simple reaction time and Go/No-Go tasks. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test, with rank-biserial correlation used to estimate effect size. Levene's test assessed differences in variability, and kurtosis was calculated for RT. Exploratory multiple regression analyses examined associations between cognitive outcomes and disposition, mood, sleep quality, and tension. No statistically significant between-group differences were observed for RT, DT, AT, or IC (P > .05). However, experienced dancers demonstrated significantly lower RT variability than non-dancers (F = 5.63, P = .026), with a moderate rank-biserial correlation for RT (.314) and a trend toward faster responses (256.30 ± 18.70 vs 280.15 ± 45.25 ms; P = .091). Exploratory regression analyses showed that tension was associated with AT in dancers (P = .0037), whereas disposition was associated with RT (P = .0424) and AT (P = .0147) in non-dancers. Experienced dancers exhibited greater consistency in reaction time performance and a trend toward faster responses, despite no significant differences in overall cognitive outcomes. These findings suggest that long-term dance practice may be associated with more stable sensorimotor processing and support immersive VR as a promising tool for cognitive assessment in dancers.

papers.title: Acute Encephalopathy in a Patient with Dravet Syndrome Successfully Managed with Therapeutic Normothermia and Vitamin Supplementation Therapy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Acute encephalopathy associated with Dravet syndrome (DS-AE) is a life-threatening complication associated with poor neurological outcomes. However, treatment strategies for this condition have yet to be established. Herein, we report the case of a patient with DS-AE who showed substantial neurological recovery following multidisciplinary treatment involving targeted temperature management (TTM) and vitamin supplementation, indicating the potential utility of this therapeutic approach. A 3-year-4-month-old girl with clinically diagnosed Dravet syndrome developed febrile convulsive status epilepticus associated with respiratory syncytial virus infection. Although seizures were terminated by treatment with intravenous midazolam, the patient remained comatose, and the electroencephalography demonstrated diffuse slow-wave activity, leading to a diagnosis of DS-AE. She was treated with intensive care, including continuous midazolam infusion; TTM for 48 hours; and vitamin supplementation with thiamine, pyridoxine, and L-carnitine. Despite diffuse cerebral atrophy on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the acute phase, she gradually recovered and within 4 months of the onset returned to the developmental status achieved before DS-AE onset, with subsequent improvement in cerebral atrophy on follow-up MRI. Multidisciplinary treatment, including TTM and vitamin supplementation, may represent a therapeutic strategy to reduce neurological sequelae in patients with DS-AE.

papers.title: Pathological mechanisms of the "lifestyle-immunometabolic-neuroendocrine" crosstalk network in ectopic fat deposition and skeletal muscle decline.
papers.abstract: Chronic low-grade systemic inflammation serves as a pivotal pathological link coupling unhealthy lifestyles with malignant remodeling of body composition. This review systematically constructs and elucidates the molecular mechanisms and pathological progression of the "lifestyle-immunometabolic-neuroendocrine" crosstalk network in ectopic fat deposition and skeletal muscle decline. Upstream multidimensional lifestyle stressors-including unhealthy diets, sleep deprivation, psychological stress, and sedentary behavior-disrupt the gut barrier, endocrine barriers, and mechanical contractile strain, thereby initiating immunometabolic reprogramming and triggering systemic chronic low-grade sterile inflammation. Acting as a core pathological driver, this low-grade inflammation impairs lipid and protein homeostasis, propels lipotoxic spillover and intramyocellular fat infiltration, and ultimately leads to the progressive decline of skeletal muscle mass and function. Concurrently, age-related neuroendocrine axis decline and dwindling sex hormone levels function as endogenous amplifiers, synergistically accelerating tissue microenvironmental remodeling and body composition imbalance in a distinctly dimorphic manner (e.g., postmenopausal estrogen deficiency accelerates muscle deterioration by inducing autophagy dysfunction in muscle stem cells). A deep mechanistic parsing of the regulatory nodes within this multidimensional network provides substantial academic value for deciphering the onset and progression of lifestyle-driven chronic inflammatory disorders.

papers.title: Solutions to Reduce Burnout Syndrome Among Perioperative Healthcare Providers in Low-Resource Settings: A Qualitative Study.
papers.abstract: Research from high-income countries indicates that perioperative care providers are at high risk for burnout, with potential downstream effects on patient safety. Adequate solutions to address burnout may be particularly important in low-income countries where the effects of burnout on staff motivation and migration are likely to be compounded by the current human resources crisis. This study aimed to explore solutions to address burnout among Rwandan perioperative care providers. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with perioperative care providers (obstetricians, surgeons, anesthetists, midwives, nurses) in hospitals across all five provinces in Rwanda. Interviews were analyzed using both inductive and deductive coding following standard procedures of thematic analysis. Interviews were completed with 61 participants from all levels of public hospitals (37% teaching, 6% referral, 52% district, and 5% unknown level). The participants identified solutions at multiple levels fitting within the multilevel model of burnout.At the individual level, many drew on internal values and self-developed coping mechanisms to manage occupational stress, emphasizing the importance of fulfilling basic needs such as sleep and nutrition, and stress-relief activities such as exercise and music. At the interpersonal level, support networks involving family, friends, religious communities, and colleagues played a significant role in sustaining resilience. At the hospital level, participants found motivation through positive patient outcomes. They underscored the impact of hospital organization on workload and recommended reducing inefficiencies.Regarding the healthcare system, concerns were raised about insufficient financial resources affecting staff salaries and access to essential medicines and equipment. Participants emphasized that increasing staffing levels would improve scheduling flexibility and reduce burnout. Finally, cultural factors such as recognition, appreciation, and respectful workplace interactions were deemed essential for morale. This study illustrates that resilience among healthcare professionals is shaped by a complex interplay of individual, interpersonal, institutional, and systemic factors. While many rely on personal values and coping strategies to manage the demands of clinical work, their resilience is often strained by unmet basic needs, geographic isolation, organizational inefficiencies, and broader systemic limitations such as inadequate staffing and financing. Cultural dynamics, including recognition, respect, and workplace relationships, further influence the capacity to cope with stress. To address burnout effectively, solutions must be adapted to the Rwandan context and implemented at all levels, ranging from promoting self-care and peer support to improving hospital management and resource allocation, and to promoting innovative and evidence-based interventions.
